labels.definition: Sections featuring the creation, fall, or repentance of Adam, or his sons.
A truthful prophet raised to a high station; pre-Flood.
The Flood narrative, Noah's da'wah, his son, or his prayer.
Prophet sent to 'Ad; warns of their destruction by a barren wind.
Prophet sent to Thamud; the she-camel sign; the rock-cut homes.
Abraham's monotheism, breaking idols, the sacrifice, his prayer for Mecca.
Abraham's son; granted as a prophet, often paired with Jacob.
Abraham's eldest son; true to his promise; co-builder of the Ka'bah.
Lot's people, their corruption, their destruction.
The patriarch (also called Israel); Abraham's grandson; father of Joseph.
The Joseph narrative (almost entirely Surah Yusuf).
Prophet sent to Madyan; warned them against fraud in trade and short-measuring.
Moses's call, confrontation with Pharaoh, the Exodus, his time at Sinai.
Moses's brother; appointed prophet alongside him, often co-mentioned.
A patient prophet mentioned briefly alongside Ishmael and Idris; tradition associates him variably with Ezekiel or Isaiah.
David's kingship, his judgment between disputants, his psalms.
Solomon's kingdom, his control over jinn/wind/animals, Queen of Sheba.
Prophet who called his people away from worshipping Ba'al.
Prophet mentioned in brief lists of the favored.
Jonah's flight, the fish, his repentance.
Job's affliction and steadfast patience.
Zechariah's secret prayer for an heir; the sign of muteness; his guardianship of Mary.
John's birth, his given character — wisdom as a child, dutifulness, God-consciousness.
Mary as a subject — her devotion, the annunciation, her trial.
The conception, miracles, ministry, or theological status of Jesus.
Sections directly addressing the Prophet, his role, or his domestic life.
The household of Imran, especially Mary's mother, Mary, and the chosen lineage named in Surah Al-Imran.
The disciples of Jesus who profess support for Allah and His messenger.
Pharaoh as antagonist — his court, his magicians, his drowning.
The king appointed for the Children of Israel before David's victory over Goliath.
The opposing warrior defeated by David in the Saul narrative.
The refusal to prostrate, the whispering, the tempter's role.
The people of Hud — known for might; destroyed by a barren wind.
The people of Salih — carvers of mountain dwellings; destroyed by the cry / earthquake after slaying the she-camel.
The people of Shuayb — destroyed for fraud in trade.
The traveler-king narrative and Gog & Magog.
The narrative of the youths in the cave.
Bani Israel as collective subject — covenant, rebellion, prophets sent to them.
The patriarchal tribes or descendants named alongside Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and Jesus in revelation lists.
Jews and Christians addressed collectively.
The Sabeans as a named religious community listed with believers, Jews, and Christians.
Sections about the Munafiqun — their behavior, their fate, their identification.
Direct address to believers (`yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū`) as the rhetorical subject.
Universal address to all humanity (`yā ayyuhā an-nās`). A finite, identifiable set; high-value filter for users wanting every passage addressed to humans as such.
Disbelievers as collective subject — their arguments, their fate, their accusations.
Mushrikun specifically — those associating partners with God.
Sections aimed at the early Meccan opposition.
Angels as collective subject, including Gabriel/Jibril when not separately named.
The two angels named in the Babylon sorcery passage.
Jinn as collective subject.
Sections asserting God's absolute oneness or refuting associates/sons.
God's mercy, forgiveness, and compassion as the dominant theme.
God's justice, fair judgment, never wronging by an atom's weight.
God as King, owner of dominion, holder of all power.
God's complete knowledge of the seen and unseen.
God's omnipotence and ability over all things.
God's wise ordering of events, decree, and law.
God as Creator — bringing into being, originating.
God as sustainer who provides rizq to all creatures.
God as the source of guidance, sender of guidance, light through darkness.
God as near, hearing, responding to those who call.
God's decree, predestination, the lawh mahfuz, what He has written.
Uttered supplication asking for forgiveness or removal of sin.
Asking to be guided to or kept on the straight path.
Calling on God in hardship, fear, or persecution.
Asking for righteous offspring, spouses, or family.
Asking for understanding, wisdom, or eloquence.
Seeking refuge from evil, satanic suggestion, calamity, hell.
Supplications that thank or praise God for a blessing or favor.
Rules of marriage, treatment of spouses, family conduct.
Rules of divorce, iddah, custody, separation.
Distribution of estate and inheritance shares.
Rules of fighting, peace agreements, conduct during conflict.
Leaving home or being expelled for Allah's cause; the moral and legal status of emigrants.
Commerce, contracts, debt, witnessing.
Sections legislating against or warning about riba — usury, interest, and unjust gain through lending.
Wine/intoxicants, gambling, games of chance, and their social or spiritual harms.
What is permitted and forbidden to eat; slaughter rules.
Wudu, ghusl, menstruation, ritual cleanliness.
Establishment of salah, its times, its conduct.
Rules and virtues of fasting, primarily Ramadan.
The pilgrimage, its rites, the sacred precincts.
The Sacred Mosque, qiblah direction, and sanctuary-linked orientation or access rules.
Obligatory zakat, voluntary sadaqah, spending in God's cause.
Care, protection, fair treatment, and property rights of orphans.
Freeing slaves, ransom, captives, and liberation-linked obligations or virtues.
Swearing, breaking oaths, expiation.
Covenants, solemn pledges, and binding commitments between Allah and people or among people.
Bearing witness, just judgment between people, slander cases.
Commendation or modeling of steadfast patience under trial.
Commendation of thankfulness, recognition of God's favors.
The disposition of being mindful of God; the muttaqun.
Reliance on God in decision and outcome.
Turning back to God, the door of repentance, accepting the repentant.
Lowering oneself before God or fellow humans; rejecting pride.
Acting purely for God's sake, free of ostentation.
Remembering God by tongue or heart; the role of dhikr in calming the heart.

Sections containing explicit praise or glorification of God — `al-ḥamdu lillāh`, `tabāraka`, `subḥān`, `Allāhu akbar`. Distinct from `gratitude` (which marks shukr for specific blessings) and from divine-attribute labels (which mark the attribute being praised). Apply when praise is *uttered* in the section, not merely commanded.
Broad ethical conduct toward parents, neighbors, the poor — the "righteousness" passages.
Pride that refuses truth or despises people; Iblis's defining flaw.
The trait of professing belief outwardly while disbelieving inwardly.
Scheming and conspiracy against truth or against the believers; God's counter-plan.
Associating partners with God in worship, lordship, or attributes.
Mocking the believers, the Prophet, or revelation; mocking past prophets.
Spreading false accusations, gossiping, defamation.
Hoarding, refusing to spend in God's cause, love of wealth.
Magic, witchcraft, sorcery accusations, or the practice and teaching of sihr.
Unjust killing, wrath-driven action, the sin of Cain.
Resenting blessings God has given another; explicit refuge sought from it.
Causing fasād — moral, social, or material corruption.
The state of denying truth after it has reached one.
The Day described — its terror, its arrangement, the standing before God.
Descriptions of Jannah — its rivers, gardens, companions, rewards.
Descriptions of Jahannam — its punishments, its keepers, its inhabitants.
The raising of the dead, the trumpet, the gathering.
Cosmic signs preceding the Hour — sun darkened, mountains scattered.
The handing of records, weighing of deeds, accounting.
Who may intercede, who may not, on the Day.
The destruction of 'Ad, Thamud, Pharaoh's people, Lot's people as warning.
The making of the cosmos in six days; the throne.
Stages of human creation — clay, sperm, clot, lump.
Rain, plants, wind, animals, the tame earth, birds in flight — earthly natural phenomena framed as signs of the Creator. Co-tag with `cosmic-bodies` when both are present.

Celestial bodies — sun, moon, stars, lamps of heaven, night, day — framed as signs or as adornment of the heavens. Distinct from `natural-signs` and freely co-tagged with it; both apply when both are present in the section.
The reality of death, the taking of the soul, what comes after.
Generic ruins-and-warnings — "have they not traveled the land?"
Sections where the Qur'an is itself the subject — its origin, character, preservation.

Sections opening with the disjoined Arabic letters — Alif-Lām-Mīm, Ḥā-Mīm, Kāf-Hā-Yā-ʿAyn-Ṣād, Yā-Sīn, Ṭā-Hā, etc. Tag whenever the section begins with one of these openings, regardless of tafsir interpretation.

Sections containing the rhetorical pattern `Qul…` ("Say…") — God commanding the Prophet (or, in some sections, the believers) to declare or recite a specific statement. Tag whenever the imperative `qul` appears. Use this **instead of** `muhammad` for the "Say:" pattern; `muhammad` is reserved for direct second-person address or sections substantively about him.
Torah, Gospel, Psalms as subjects; their relationship to the Qur'an.
Prophethood as a category — the sending of messengers, their common message.
Miraculous signs given to prophets (Moses's staff, Jesus's healings, the splitting of the moon).
The Qur'anic challenge to produce a chapter or verse like it.
Accusations that the Qur'an is poetry, magic, or fabrication, and the responses.
